Wee Hur secures option to buy Sydney student accommodation site
article:
Wee Hur Holdings has secured an unconditional option for the proposed acquisition of a 2,744 sq m (29,536 sq ft) student accommodation site in Sydney, Australia, for an undisclosed amount.

“The purchase is expected to be completed in 2H2027, subject to the exercise of the option and completion of the transaction in accordance with its terms,” the Singapore-listed company stated in an Oct 20 bourse filing.

The site, located at 35 to 51 Nicholson Street in Wollstonecraft, Sydney, is earmarked for a 12-storey purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) with 471 beds.

The development will offer studios, ensuite rooms and two-bedroom apartments, along with communal indoor and outdoor living spaces and other resident amenities.

Wee Hur says it plans to bring in external capital partners for the project, which will be held through a special purpose vehicle (SPV). Wee Hur will retain an equity interest in the SPV, subject to finalisation of the investment structure.

The development will be undertaken by Wee Hur Capital, while Intergen Property Group will serve as the project's local investment manager.

Upon completion, the group plans to operate the property under its Y Suites student accommodation brand.

The proposed development will add to Wee Hur’s PBSA platform, which has been steadily expanding.

In Australia, the group’s portfolio includes Y Suites on Margaret in Sydney, a 409-bed operational property, and Y Suites on Frome in Adelaide, a 708-bed development targeted for completion in 4Q2027.

Earlier this year in June, the group entered the Hong Kong PBSA market through a joint venture with Starvia Holdings. The joint venture will operate the 246-bed Starvia by Y Suites on Fortress Hill.

That same month, Wee Hur announced its acquisition of One Bedford Place , a 26-storey office building in Tai Kok Tsui, Kowloon, which it plans to convert into a 500-bed PBSA.

Last month, the group announced its entry into Singapore’s PBSA market with a proposed 1,398-bed development at Nanyang Technological University.

Goh Wee Ping, CEO of Wee Hur Capital and chief investment officer of Wee Hur Holdings, said the group is becoming “increasingly selective” about where it invests, amid a “cautiously optimistic” outlook on the Australian student accommodation market.

“[The site at Nicholson Street] is a good example of what we look for – a well-connected location, convenient access to major universities and an established neighbourhood with the amenities that students value,” he added.

The site is a three-minute walk from the Crows Nest Metro station. Retail and dining amenities are within walking distance, while the North Sydney commercial district is five minutes away by public transport.

It is also close to several universities, including the University of Sydney, the University of Technology Sydney and Macquarie University.

title: Walmart sweetens subscription plan to win online shoppers
article:
(Oct 20): Walmart Inc is bundling its online subscription program with a Sam’s Club membership to lure shoppers from Amazon Prime and other competitors.

Consumers can now get both Walmart+ and Sam’s Club Plus together for US$120 a year. Separately, the two memberships cost nearly US$100 more than that amount.

Walmart has been looking at ways to offer new savings as costs have risen in recent years, chief executive officer John Furner said in an interview on Tuesday with Bloomberg News.

Members of the subscription programs have asked for this type of benefit for some time and will now get new perks. The company plans to take their feedback to decide how to update the offerings going forward, Furner said.

“As you hear more about cost of living and costs all over, this is a big saving,” he said, adding that Walmart wanted to start offering the package before the holiday season. “We hear a pretty high number of people who are planning earlier than last year. We also know that there are a lot of last-minute gifts in the market every year.”

See also: LVMH sales at key unit fall as China woes hurt Louis Vuitton

Similar to Amazon.com Inc’s Prime, Walmart+ offers free online delivery as well as streaming services, gas savings and other benefits for almost US$100 a year, or US$13 per month.

Sam’s Club, a warehouse club chain owned by Walmart with about 600 US locations, offers two tiers of membership, with the more expensive Plus version costing US$120 annually. Members get free delivery and 2% cash back along with additional perks.

The bundling of Sam’s Club membership with Walmart+ shows how the big-box retailer seeks to capture market share by offering value as sustained inflation sends shoppers on a hunt for deals. It’s a package that competitors will be hard-pressed to match, given no other US retailer owns a big-box operator, a warehouse chain and an integrated e-commerce business.

See also: The bricks-and-mortar store’s next biggest challenge is selling itself

Shoppers will still have the option to purchase memberships separately. Walmart employees will get both memberships for free as part of their benefits.

Amazon Prime costs US$140 a year, or US$15 per month, while premium subscription plans from Target Corp and Kroger both cost US$100 annually.

Paid memberships have become a more significant driver of growth for retailers. Users tend to spend more and become loyal customers, while fees help boost profits. Amazon, which pioneered the model, remains the biggest player. About 200 million people in the US have access to a Prime membership.

Walmart has said its subscription plan is growing, without disclosing how many members it has. In August, the company said Walmart+ had the best first half of membership growth in its history and reported that membership income grew nearly 17% globally. Sam’s Club has succeeded in attracting younger shoppers with its business model.

Declining consumer sentiment has sparked intense competition among retailers. This trend has largely favoured Walmart, which has built its business on ensuring prices are low. The Bentonville, Arkansas-based retailer has attracted shoppers across income groups in recent years — especially wealthier ones. It has also expanded its selection of goods while offering faster delivery for online orders.

Furner, who took over in February, has said that the company is investing heavily in keeping its low prices as consumers seek out value. This strategy will lead to market-share gains over time, he has said.

title: US housing starts fall to four-month low as demand falters
article:
(Oct 20): New US residential construction declined in September to a four-month low and building permits for single-family homes slid, highlighting a struggling housing market.

Housing starts decreased 5.2% to an annualised rate of 1.22 million, according to federal government data released on Tuesday. The pace trailed all estimates in a Bloomberg survey of economists.

Starts of single-family homes decreased 4.6% to the lowest level in a year, while new construction on multifamily projects fell nearly 7%.

Permit applications for one-family homes, a gauge of future construction, dropped to the lowest since early 2023.

The residential real estate market is being constrained by affordability challenges now further compounded by higher mortgage rates. Homebuilders, whose confidence has slumped to a 14-year low, may also be reluctant to begin construction on new homes before making more progress on inventories.

Sluggish home construction has weighed on economic growth in five of the last six quarters. Before Tuesday’s report, the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta’s GDPNow forecast pencilled in residential investment declining an annualised 1.3% in the third quarter.
